read.sections.0.heading.source: A letter writer in colonial Java
read.sections.0.heading.back: A letter writer in colonial Java

read.sections.0.text.source: Raden Ajeng Kartini was born in 1879 in Jepara, on the island of Java. At that time, the Netherlands ruled Java as a colony. Her father was a local leader, and she went to school until she was about 12. That was more schooling than most girls in Java had. Then, like other girls from noble families, she had to stay at home until she married. She kept reading, and she wrote many letters, mostly in Dutch, to friends. She wrote about why girls should be able to learn and choose their own path. A letter shows one person's hopes. It cannot speak for every girl in Java. Today her letters are kept in archives in the Netherlands and Indonesia.
read.sections.0.text.back: Raden Ajeng Kartini was born in 1879 in Jepara on the island of Java. At that time the Netherlands ruled Java as a colony. Her father was a local leader, and she went to school until about age 12, more than most girls in Java got to study. Then she had to stay at home until marriage, like other girls from noble families. She kept reading, and wrote letters to many friends, mostly in Dutch. She wrote about why girls should be able to study and choose their own path in life. The letters show one person's hopes. They cannot speak for every girl in Java. Today her letters are kept in archives in the Netherlands and Indonesia.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Kartini was born in 1879 on the island of Java. The Netherlands ruled Java then. Her father was a local leader. She went to school until she was about 12. Then she had to stay at home. She wrote many letters to friends. She wrote that girls should be able to learn. A letter shows what one person hoped. It does not speak for every girl. Today her letters are kept in an archive.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Kartini was born in 1879 on the island of Java. At that time the Netherlands ruled Java. Her father was a local leader. She went to school until about age 12. Then she had to stay at home. She wrote many letters to friends. She wrote that girls should be able to study. The letters show what one person hoped. The letters do not speak for every girl. Today her letters are kept in archives.

read.sections.1.text.source: In October 1901, Kartini wrote a long letter to a friend. She wrote that she and her sisters hoped to open a school one day. It would teach more than books: handwork, cooking, wood-carving and painting too. In the same letter, she wrote about a different plan. The colonial government was planning schools for girls, and Kartini had been asked to teach in one. These were two plans, not one. We can read her letter in an English translation from 1921. Years after her death, an editor chose which letters to print, and the English book kept only some of them.
read.sections.1.text.back: In October 1901, Kartini wrote a long letter to a friend. She wrote that she and her sisters hoped one day to open a school. This school would teach more than reading: crafts, cooking, woodcarving and drawing too. In the same letter, she wrote about another plan. The colonial government was planning to set up schools for girls, and Kartini had been approached to teach at one. These are two plans, not one. We can read her letter in an English translation from 1921, years after she died. An editor chose which letters to print, and the English book kept only some of them.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: In 1901, Kartini wrote a long letter. She and her sisters hoped to open a school. It would teach books, and also cooking and art. In the same letter, she wrote about another plan. The government planned schools for girls. It asked Kartini to teach. These were two different plans. We read the letter in an English translation from 1921. An editor chose which letters to print. So we do not have all her words.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: In 1901, Kartini wrote a long letter. She and her sisters hoped to open a school. The school would teach reading, and teach cooking and art too. In the same letter, she wrote about another plan. The government planned to set up schools for girls. The government asked Kartini to teach. These are two different plans. We read the letter in an English translation from 1921. An editor chose which letters to print, so we do not read all her words.

read.sections.2.text.source: On 7 July 1903, the colonial government made a decision. It offered Kartini and her sister Roekmini a scholarship, money to study in Batavia, the city now called Jakarta. A record of this decision is kept in Indonesia's national archive. A decision shows what officials agreed to at one moment. It does not prove that anyone used the money. In fact, the sisters did not use it, and later that year Kartini married. The second picture is her portrait, printed in a book in 1922, long after her death. It shows her face, not her thoughts.
read.sections.2.text.back: On 7 July 1903, the colonial government made a decision. It offered a scholarship to Kartini and her sister Roekmini: money to go and study in Batavia, the city now called Jakarta. The record of this decision is kept in the National Archives of Indonesia. A decision shows what officials agreed at one time, but does not prove anyone used the money. In fact the two sisters did not use the money, and at the end of that year Kartini married. The second picture is a portrait of her printed in a book in 1922, long after she died. It shows her face, not her thoughts.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: On 7 July 1903, the government made a decision. It gave Kartini and her sister a scholarship. This was money to study in Batavia, now called Jakarta. An archive in Indonesia keeps the decision. A decision shows what leaders agreed. It does not show what happened next. The sisters did not use the money. The second picture is a portrait of Kartini. It was printed in 1922. It shows her face, not her thoughts.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: On 7 July 1903, the government made a decision. It gave a scholarship to Kartini and her sister. This was money to go and study in Batavia, which is now called Jakarta. An archive in Indonesia keeps this decision. The decision shows what leaders agreed, but does not show what happened next. The two sisters did not use the money. The second picture is a portrait of Kartini. It was printed in 1922. It shows her face, not her thoughts.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Kartini's life touches on things that can be personal: girls kept at home, arranged marriage (her husband already had other wives), and her death a few days after giving birth. The lesson says only that she married in 1903; if the rest comes up, keep it brief and factual. Many learners have had their own schooling interrupted: keep the lesson on Kartini's sources, and never ask learners whether they or girls they know were kept out of school or married young, or about their own or their family's schooling, journeys, country, religion or ethnicity.
sensitiveNotes.0.note: Teachers' note on arranged marriage (การคลุมถุงชน), polygamy and death after childbirth kept as factual and brief as the English. Learners' text says only that she married.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Kartini's life involves things that may be personal, such as girls who had to stay at home, an arranged marriage (her husband already had other wives) and her death a few days after giving birth. The lesson says only that she married in 1903. If other things come up in discussion, keep it short and factual. Many learners have had to stop school partway. Keep the lesson on Kartini's sources, and do not ask learners whether they or girls they know were kept from school or married young, or ask about their own or their family's education, journeys, country, religion or ethnicity.

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners keep Kartini's 1901 hope, the 1903 government decision and what actually happened apart, and name a limit of an edited, translated letter. Evidence move (brief 3B): keep the sisters' 1901 school hope separate from the government's plan for girls' schools (in the same letter) and from the 1903 decision. A sound answer keeps the letter's aim, the official decision and the outcome distinct. Misconceptions to catch: merging the sisters' school plan with the government plan; thinking the decision proves she studied; treating one noble woman's letters as the voice of all girls in Java. Never invent a Kartini quotation; paraphrase only. Outcome details for teachers: in July 1903 Kartini and her sisters began teaching a few girls at home; in a letter of 24 July 1903 she asked whether the unused money could go instead to a gifted young student named Salim; she married the regent of Rembang later that year and died in 1904.
educatorNotes.0.back: Goal: learners separate Kartini's hopes in 1901, the government's decision in 1903 and what really happened, and can state the limits of selected and translated letters. Evidence skill (brief 3B): separate the sisters' 1901 hope for a school from the government's plan for girls' schools (in the same letter) and from the 1903 decision. A good answer clearly separates the goal in the letter, the official decision and the outcome. Misconceptions to watch for: merging the sisters' school plan with the government's plan, thinking the decision proves she went to study, and treating one noblewoman's letters as the voice of all girls in Java. Don't invent words for Kartini; paraphrase only. Outcome details for teachers: in July 1903 Kartini and her sisters began teaching a few girls at home. In her letter of 24 July 1903 she asked whether the unused money could go instead to a talented young student named Salim. She married the ruler of Rembang at the end of that year and died in 1904.

educatorNotes.1.source: Source caveats: the 1921 English edition is a selection of about two-thirds of the 1911 Dutch book, which J.H. Abendanon edited; it carries colonial-era framing from the translator and a foreword, and the Dutch editor notes that some letters from mid-1903 were “not suitable for publication”. Separate Kartini's words from the editors'. Joost Coté's Kartini: The Complete Writings 1898–1904 (2014) is a fuller modern translation. The decision's details (7 July 1903, 4,800 guilders, study in Batavia for Kartini and Roekmini, not used) come from that Dutch edition; the National Archives of Indonesia's catalogue record of it could not be opened from here.
educatorNotes.1.back: Source caution: the 1921 English edition is a selection of about two thirds of the 1911 Dutch book edited by J.H. Abendanon. It carries colonial-era framing from the translator and introduction, and the Dutch editor noted that some letters from mid-1903 were "not suitable for publication". Separate Kartini's words from the editor's words. Joost Coté's Kartini: The Complete Writings 1898–1904 (2014) is a more complete modern translation. The decision's details (7 July 1903, 4,800 guilders, for Kartini and Roekmini to study in Batavia, and not used) come from that Dutch edition. The National Archives of Indonesia catalogue entry about this cannot be opened from here.
